title: The best way to watch the Olympics
author: David Pierce

recommendations.name: Peacock’s Gold Zone
recommendations.blurb: This is not strictly a new thing, really, just a PSA: For my money there is no better way to watch the Olympics than through Gold Zone, which whips around the Games to show you the most interesting thing happening at any given moment.

recommendations.name: Raindrop.io Stella
recommendations.blurb: A big AI-powered update to my favorite bookmarking app. So far, it’s what you’d expect: a much better way to search, ask questions about, and otherwise interact with your bookmarks. After trying a bunch of other apps, I’ve been back in on Raindrop recently, and this comes at the perfect time.

recommendations.name: Super Nintendo
recommendations.blurb: I really don’t think there’s another company quite like Nintendo. Keza MacDonald’s book is a business story, a game story, and more besides — I’ve only just started reading it and I’ve already learned a ton. (Stay tuned, by the way: we have an excertp from the book running on the site on Monday.)

recommendations.name: Codex for Mac
recommendations.blurb: OpenAI’s answer to Claude Code got a desktop app, and I’ve been hearing pretty good things about it. I’m particularly intrigued by the Automations feature, which I intend to use to help clean up my Downloads folder every week or so.

recommendations.name: The Muppet Show
recommendations.blurb: The Muppets were such a big part of my childhood, and it’s so weird that my own kids have barely seen them. This new special is both modern — Sabrina Carpenter and Seth Rogen are in it! — and perfectly timeless. I’m going to make my kids watch it 65,000 times.

recommendations.name: You are being misled about renewable energy technology
recommendations.blurb: “ You are being misled about renewable energy technology.” After hearing Alec on the great State of the Workflow series, I’ve been watching a lot of Technology Connections. This one is rightly going viral, because it’s a rare mix of totally reasonable and utterly infuriating.

recommendations.name: Dragon Quest VII Reimagined
recommendations.blurb: I swear, once a week someone ships a remastered game that makes me go “Oh, man, I forgot about that game!” Somehow this series is 40 years old, and though the cartoony screenshots don’t totally do it for me, I suspect a lot of folks will have a blast digging back into this one.

recommendations.name: The RetroVa Vintage Imaging Kit
recommendations.blurb: Yes, it’s a Kickstarter, so proceed with caution. But: We’ve seen this company’s smartphone camera lens extenders work on Vivo and Oppo phones, so there’s good reason to believe this kit will work well on iPhones too. (Bummer that a lot of features look like they require a proprietary app, though.)

recommendations.name: Queen of Chess
recommendations.blurb: Before this documentary hit Netflix, I confess I knew almost nothing about Judit Polgár, who in 1991 became the youngest chess grandmaster ever. Her story is remarkable, and so is the way chess is depicted in this film — very Queen’s Gambit, in the best way.

recommendations.name: Chronicles of a Liquid Society
recommendations.blurb: I’m reading Chronicles of a Liquid Society, the last book from Umberto Eco. A collection of his editorials that read like blog posts. They range from 2000 onward, so some of the topics are now quaint (like the implausible idea in 2004 that every kid has a computer in class).

recommendations.name: BBC Archive’s YouTube channel
recommendations.blurb: Last week, thanks to Chris Mims, I spent some time on the BBC Archive’s YouTube channel.

recommendations.name: clips from the old Top Gear crew
recommendations.blurb: When I haven’t been enjoying a treasure trove of well-curated clips from the old Top Gear crew, I’ve been watching a ton of old news clips from the early days of personal computing and the internet.
